title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F09
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 10 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 60 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Find an EOdashboard narrative about environmental changes observed from space during the Covid-19 lockdown (such as improved air quality, clearer waterways, or reduced maritime traffic), identify the affected study area, then download two Sentinel-2 true-colour images of that area — one from approximately one year before the lockdown (same season, 2019) and one from during the lockdown (2020) — and compare the two images to assess whether visible environmental changes are apparent.

answers.text:
Based on the visual comparison of the two Sentinel-2 true-color images of Milan, Italy:

1.  Image from March-May 2019 (Pre-lockdown): The image shows the city with its typical urban density, including visible road networks, buildings, and surrounding agricultural areas. The overall appearance is consistent with normal urban activity.

2.  Image from March-May 2020 (During Lockdown): The image from the same season and location during the lockdown period shows a very similar urban landscape. The city's structure, including buildings, roads, and surrounding areas, appears largely unchanged.

Conclusion:

While the EO Dashboard narrative identified a significant 50% reduction in nitrogen dioxide (NO2) levels in Milan during the lockdown, this reduction is an atmospheric measurement, not a direct visual change in the urban landscape captured by the Sentinel-2 satellite. The true-color images from 2019 and 2020 do not show any obvious visible changes in the city's physical appearance, such as reduced traffic congestion or altered land use patterns, which would be expected from a major reduction in human activity. The visual comparison confirms that the environmental change observed was primarily atmospheric (air quality) rather than a visible alteration in the urban environment from this satellite perspective.

Based on the visual comparison of the two Sentinel-2 true-colour images of Delhi, India, taken in March 2019 (pre-lockdown) and March 2020 (during the COVID-19 lockdown), the following observations can be made:

1.  Overall Visual Similarity: The two images are remarkably similar in terms of the urban layout, the distribution of green areas (vegetation), and the course of the rivers. The major roads, buildings, and infrastructure appear to be in the same locations in both images.

2.  Air Quality and Atmospheric Clarity: The most significant difference is in the atmospheric clarity. The March 2020 image appears to have a slightly hazy or smoggy overlay, particularly noticeable over the central and eastern parts of the city. This is consistent with the findings from the research papers, which indicated a significant reduction in air pollution during the lockdown period. The haze in the 2020 image is likely due to a combination of factors, including the reduction in vehicular and industrial emissions, which typically leads to clearer air, and the potential for increased atmospheric particulate matter from other sources (like dust or biomass burning) during the lockdown period.

3.  Urban Activity: The images do not show any significant changes in the density of urban activity, such as the number of vehicles or construction sites. This is expected, as the lockdown measures were implemented to reduce human movement and activity, but the images were taken during the same season (March) in both years, and the lockdown measures were not fully implemented in March 2020 until later in the month.

In conclusion, the visual comparison of the two images suggests that the COVID-19 lockdown had a significant impact on air quality in Delhi, India, with a reduction in air pollution during the lockdown period. The images provide a clear visual representation of the changes in air quality and atmospheric clarity between the two periods.

Based on the visual comparison of the two Sentinel-2 true-colour images for the Northeast United States study area (bounding box: [-78.0, 38.0, -70.0, 43.0]):

1.  Pre-lockdown Image (March 15–April 15, 2019): The image shows a typical urban and natural landscape with visible cloud cover and some areas of darker, possibly forested or less developed land. The water bodies (like the Atlantic Ocean and the coastlines) appear as dark blue/black areas.

2.  During Lockdown Image (March 15–April 15, 2020): The image appears visually similar to the pre-lockdown image, with comparable cloud cover and land/water features. There are no obvious, large-scale, visible changes in land use, vegetation, or water clarity that can be directly attributed to the lockdown period from this true-colour perspective.

Conclusion:
While the EO Dashboard narrative indicates a ~30% reduction in nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) levels in this region during the lockdown, this reduction is not visually apparent in the true-colour Sentinel-2 imagery. True-colour images primarily capture reflected sunlight in the visible spectrum (red, green, blue), which does not directly show atmospheric pollutants like NO₂. To observe such changes, specialized data (like the NO₂ data from the N1_NO2 collection) or false-colour composites would be required. The visual comparison confirms that the most prominent changes during the lockdown, as observed from space, are not visible in standard true-colour imagery.

items.question: Find the EO Dashboard narrative about extreme air pollution episodes in Northern India and Pakistan, identify a representative city discussed in the narrative, and retrieve Sentinel-5P atmospheric composition data for that location during the smog season. Describe the spatial distribution of pollutant concentrations and explain how the observations relate to the pollution episode described in the narrative.

answers.text:
Based on the EO Dashboard narrative and the Sentinel-5P atmospheric data for Delhi, India, here is the analysis of the extreme air pollution episode:

Representative City:
The narrative "Extreme air pollution episodes in Northern India and Pakistan" identifies the Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP) as the primary region of concern, encompassing Northern India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. While it does not focus on a single specific city, Delhi, India, is a representative urban center within this region and is well-documented for its severe winter smog episodes.

Spatial Distribution of Pollutant Concentrations:
The Sentinel-5P NO2 data for Delhi during the smog season (November-December 2023) reveals a distinct spatial pattern:
• The image shows NO2 column concentrations in greyscale, with brighter areas indicating higher concentrations.
• The urban core of Delhi exhibits significantly elevated NO2 levels, appearing as bright spots in the image.
• This pattern is consistent with the narrative's description of intense industrial and agricultural activities in the IGP, which contribute to high pollution levels.
• The spatial distribution highlights the concentration of pollution in urban areas, with lower concentrations observed in surrounding rural regions.

Relation to the Pollution Episode:
The observations directly correlate with the pollution episode described in the narrative:
• The high NO2 concentrations in Delhi's urban core align with the narrative's focus on the IGP as a region of intense pollution.
• The winter smog season in Delhi is characterized by temperature inversions that trap pollutants near the surface, leading to the observed high concentrations.
• The data visually confirms the narrative's assertion that the region experiences severe air pollution episodes, posing significant health risks to the local population.
• The spatial distribution of pollutants underscores the impact of urbanization and industrial activities on air quality in the IGP region.

In summary, the Sentinel-5P data for Delhi provides concrete evidence of the extreme air pollution episode described in the EO Dashboard narrative, demonstrating the spatial concentration of pollutants in urban areas and validating the narrative's findings about the health risks associated with poor air quality in the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

items.question: An EO Dashboard narrative discusses long-term warming trends. List the available CDS datasets to identify which ones provide future climate projections and seasonal forecasts.

answers.text:
After a thorough search in the EO Dashboard STAC Catalog, I found that there are no datasets explicitly labeled as "future climate projections" or "seasonal forecasts" in the available collections.

However, I did find two collections labeled as "CDS" (Copernicus Data Store) that provide ERA5 reanalysis data for wind fields at 100m globally. These datasets are:

1. CDS7
• Title: CDS7
• Themes: Atmosphere
• URL: CDS7 Collection (https://esa-eodashdashboard.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/windu_ERA5-SingleLevel_100m_GLOBAL/collection.json)
• Description: This collection provides ERA5 reanalysis data for the U-component of wind at 100m globally.
• Sample Data:
  • Wind U Field at 100m (e.g., VIS_ERA5_SINGLELEVEL_WIND_U_100M_GLOBAL)
  • Temporal Coverage: Multiple time slices (e.g., 2023-12-27 to 2023-12-31)
  • Spatial Coverage: Global (Lon: -180 to 180, Lat: -90.22 to 90)
• Items: 365+ items available.

2. CDS8
• Title: CDS8
• Themes: Atmosphere
• URL: CDS8 Collection (https://esa-eodashdashboard.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/windv_ERA5-SingleLevel_100m_GLOBAL/collection.json)
• Description: This collection provides ERA5 reanalysis data for the V-component of wind at 100m globally.
• Sample Data:
  • Wind V Field at 100m (e.g., VIS_ERA5_SINGLELEVEL_WIND_V_100M_GLOBAL)
  • Temporal Coverage: Multiple time slices (e.g., 2023-12-27 to 2023-12-31)
  • Spatial Coverage: Global (Lon: -180 to 180, Lat: -90.22 to 90)
• Items: 365+ items available.

Key Notes:
• These datasets are reanalysis products, not future climate projections or seasonal forecasts.
• They provide historical wind data at 100m globally, which can be useful for climate studies but do not include future projections or seasonal forecasts.
• If you are specifically looking for future climate projections or seasonal forecasts, you may need to explore other sources like the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS) directly or other climate-specific datasets.

Would you like me to search for other climate-related datasets or assist further?

The EO Dashboard narratives and STAC catalog do not explicitly list Climate Data Store (CDS) datasets for future climate projections or seasonal forecasts under the available themes or keywords.

If you are interested in future climate projections or seasonal forecasts, these may be available through:
• Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS) directly (not explicitly listed in the EO Dashboard).
• Narratives or scientific literature within the EO Dashboard that discuss climate projections.

Would you like me to:
1. Search for narratives in the EO Dashboard that discuss climate projections or seasonal forecasts?
2. Explore other themes or datasets that might indirectly provide this information?

The EO Dashboard narratives discussing warming trends are associated with observational datasets (such as sea ice concentration and chlorophyll concentration). However, for future climate projections and seasonal forecasts, you need to access the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) via the Climate Data Store (CDS).

The relevant datasets for your needs are:

• Future Climate Projections (Long-term):
    • CMIP6 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6): Provides global simulations under various Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs) for temperature, precipitation, and wind.
    • CORDEX (Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment): Provides high-resolution regional projections by downscaling global CMIP models.

• Seasonal Forecasts (Short-term):
    • C3S Seasonal Forecasts: Provides probabilistic predictions (typically up to 6–12 months) for variables such as 2m temperature, precipitation, and sea-level pressure.

The EO Dashboard STAC catalog does not directly include future climate projections or seasonal forecasts. However, I can:

1. Search the EO Dashboard narratives for stories or analyses that discuss long-term warming trends and identify which external datasets (e.g., Copernicus Climate Data Store, CMIP6, or other climate models) they reference.
2. Guide you on accessing external climate datasets like those from the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS), NASA, or IPCC.

Would you like me to proceed with searching the narratives?

The user asked for two things:
1. An EO Dashboard narrative discussing long-term warming trends.
2. A list of available CDS datasets for future climate projections and seasonal forecasts.

The eo_stac_agent returned a relevant narrative: "Glacier monitoring under global warming trends through remote sensing – An example from The Third Pole" (and two others).
The cdse_agent stated it doesn't have a direct tool to query the CDS catalog but provided general knowledge about CMIP6, CORDEX, CMIP5 for projections, and C3S-S2S, SEAS5 for seasonal forecasts.

Let's format the response by presenting both results.

Wait, should I just concatenate them? Yes.
I will present the EO Dashboard narrative result first, then the CDS datasets result.
Let's do it.

The CDS response indicates it does not have direct access to the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS) tools to list the datasets. However, you can visit the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS) website (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/) and use their search and filter tools to find datasets related to future climate projections and seasonal forecasts.

The image confirms the geographical extent of the region described in the narrative, allowing for a visual inspection of the urban and rural landscapes that contribute to air pollution challenges in the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

For a more detailed analysis of air-quality-relevant urban haze conditions, a higher-resolution image or data specifically focused on atmospheric pollutants (like NO2 or SO2) would be more appropriate. Covid-19 Impacts on Air Quality

In an effort to mitigate the spread of the novel coronavirus, government and public health officials have enacted various social distancing practices and other measures to limit human contact, at times placing entire countries on lockdown.
As human behavior has changed during the pandemic, ongoing measurements from Earth observing instruments have detected concurrent changes in environmental factors, such as a drop in the air pollutant nitrogen dioxide (NO2).

Data shown here from the Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI jointly developed by The Netherlands and ESA) (https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Copernicus/Sentinel-5P/Tropomi) on the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite (https://www.copernicus.eu/en) satellite and the Netherlands-Finnish instrument Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) (https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/aura/spacecraft/omi.html) on the Aura satellite (https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/aura/main/index.html), show significant drops in regional nitrogen dioxide (NO2) levels that coincide with reduced traffic and industrial activity.

The measurements presented here combine and average nitrogen dioxide data to account for variations in NO2 caused by weather, such as clouds and wind. This provides a clearer picture of the impact of human activity on NO2 levels.
In Madrid, Milan, Rome, and Paris, for example, TROPOMI data show about a 50% reduction in NO2 from March 13-April 13, 2020 compared to the same months the year before. These reductions coincide with implementation of strict quarantine measures across Europe.

Similar reductions in air pollution have been observed in the Northeast United States. From Washington, D.C. to Boston, averaged OMI NO2 column data during lockdowns in March 2020 were 30% lower than averaged data for March 2015-2019.

Here is the full content of a narrative about air quality from the EO Dashboard, focusing on COVID-19 impacts:

Narrative: Covid-19 Impacts on Air Quality

Introduction
This narrative, developed collaboratively by ESA, NASA, and JAXA, examines how COVID-19 lockdowns influenced air quality by reducing nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) levels. Satellite data from multiple missions was used to quantify these changes.

Key Findings
1. Reduction in NO₂ Levels:
   • Satellite observations from ESA’s Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI and NASA’s Aura/OMI revealed significant declines in NO₂ concentrations in regions under lockdown.
   • In Madrid, Milan, Rome, and Paris, NO₂ levels dropped by ~50% between March 13–April 13, 2020, compared to the same period in 2019.
   • In the Northeast U.S. (Washington, D.C. to Boston), NO₂ levels fell by 30% in March 2020 compared to the 2015–2019 average.

2. Methodology:
   • NO₂ data was averaged to minimize weather-related variability (e.g., clouds, wind), ensuring the observed changes reflected human activity reductions.

3. Visual Evidence:
   • Europe: Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI NO₂ measurements (http://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Copernicus/Sentinel-5P/Air_pollution_remains_low_as_Europeans_stay_at_home) (Image Credit: ESA).
   • U.S.: OMI NO₂ column observations comparing March 2015–2019 (baseline) vs. March 2020 (lockdown period).

• Satellites/Instruments:
  • Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI (ESA, Copernicus)
  • Aura/OMI (NASA)
• STAC Collections:
  • N1_NO2_trilateral: NO₂ data for trilateral regions (Europe/U.S.).
  • N1_NO₂: Global NO₂ data.

Regarding the conversion from Kelvin to Celsius, the GIS analysis server is currently optimized for GeoTIFF files and cannot perform direct arithmetic on NetCDF (.nc) files. To complete this step, you can use the following Python code with the xarray library:

import xarray as xr

files = [
    'skin_temp_2023.nc',
    'skin_temp_2024.nc'
]

for file in files:
    ds = xr.open_dataset(file)
    # Convert Kelvin to Celsius
    ds['skt'] = ds['skt'] - 273.15
    ds['skt'].attrs['units'] = 'Celsius'
    ds.to_netcdf(file)
    ds.close()
